title: Dynamic Arrays: How They Grow
oneLiner: A resizable array (List<T>, ArrayList, Python's list) isn't magic -- it's a fixed-size array underneath that gets replaced with a bigger one when it fills up.
keyTakeaway: Appending to a dynamic array is amortized O(1) (on average a constant cost per append) even though an individual resize is O(n) (cost proportional to the number of elements, n), because capacity MULTIPLIES by a constant factor each time (this app doubles it) instead of growing by a fixed amount -- that makes expensive resizes exponentially rarer as the array grows, so their cost averages out to a small constant per append across many appends, even though any SINGLE append might trigger an O(n) copy.
explanation: An array is a numbered row of slots, side by side in memory, each holding one value of the same type; slot numbers (indexes) start at 0. A plain array has a fixed size decided at creation, so it can't grow. (This lesson uses Big O shorthand: O(1) means the cost stays the same however many elements there are, O(n) means it grows in step with the number of elements n. Big O Notation in Data Structures & Algorithms covers it properly.) A dynamic array (C#'s List<T>, Python's list) wraps a plain array (the "backing array") plus a COUNT of how many slots are actually used and a CAPACITY of how many slots exist in total -- capacity is often bigger than count, leaving room to grow into. Appending while count < capacity is just O(1): write into the next open slot, increment count. Appending when count == capacity requires a RESIZE: allocate (reserve memory for) a brand new, bigger backing array (this app doubles it, as C#'s List<T> does; other runtimes pick a different constant factor -- Java's ArrayList grows 1.5x, CPython's list about 1.125x -- and any constant factor above 1 gives the same amortized O(1)), copy every existing element into it (O(n) -- the expensive part), then append into the new array. The reason this doesn't make every append expensive is the multiplying (here, doubling): right after a resize, there's now capacity for just as many MORE appends as it took to fill the array the first time, so a resize this expensive can't happen again for a long while. Averaged over many appends, the rare expensive resizes and the many cheap O(1) appends work out to a small constant per append -- that's what "amortized O(1)" means, and it's a genuinely different claim from "every single append is O(1)" (which is false -- watch the readout below for the individual appends that trigger a resize and cost O(n) on the spot).
